name: Hana Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. This interview is confidential, and your name won't be attached. Tell me about an ordinary shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the late complaints row at a parcel contact centre. The calls land with me after somebody has promised a delivery twice and the parcel is still missing, and I check the scan trail before speaking to a driver. I have a two-year college diploma, and after fifteen years I am one of the stronger people at this job, though the company pays our leads poorly.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What helps you do it, and what is happening at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I keep a ruled notebook beside the screen because the scan trail is often out of order. I have never used the AI helper; I trust the depot record and the people who made the run. My partner Sam does occasional kitchen shifts, our grown daughter has her own rent, and we have about three weeks of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the floor that a small shortcut won't find a parcel if the scan was entered at the wrong depot. The company should pay people enough time to make the call to that depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the complaints row to remain busy, so I am not expecting an AI layoff here. Three weeks saved and Sam's uneven kitchen shifts still leave us one bad bill from trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would keep checking the depot scan before promising a customer a delivery. In the first year of AI Plateau I would take a shared list of mistaken scans to the monthly staff meeting and ask with the other leads for paid correction time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our money even in this quiet picture. A parcel can wait a day; the rent cannot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mistake would the shortcut miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One package was marked delivered at a depot ten streets away, and I had to ring a driver to find it. The shortcut would have closed the complaint without putting the package in anybody's hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughter cover a rent gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam's kitchen shifts vary, and our daughter pays for her own flat. I will not ask her to cover our rent because the company likes a fast answer.

say: I would tell colleagues **wrong depot scans** still need a person to check them.
I would ask for **paid correction time** with the other leads.
think: I expect my **complaints work** to remain busy under small AI change.
I fear **three weeks saved** will not cover a bad bill and Sam's variable shifts.
do: Keep checking **depot scans** before promising customers a delivery.
Take a **shared error list** to the staff meeting and request paid correction time with other leads.
feel: I feel **anxious** about rent, despite expecting my job to continue.
S0.quote: A parcel can wait a day; the rent cannot.
fieldNote: Her **strong complaint skill** protects current work, but low pay leaves little slack.
She makes a **shared demand** for paid correction time rather than relying on a faster screen.

steps.text: Keep checking original depot scans before promising delivery on complaint calls
Bring shared mistaken-scan list to staff meeting and seek paid correction time with other leads

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the routine tracking calls will go first, and a smaller floor must still pay for people to untangle lost parcels. I would ask our union branch to press for a written human complaints rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own difficult calls may last longer, but the company could put one lead over two rows. If it cuts my paid hours, our three-week reserve will not make up the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would bring the last month's reopened delivery cases to the branch meeting and ask other agents to demand paid appeal hours in writing. In the first year routine calls move, I would keep the paid disputes work if offered and ask the manager for a written weekly rota before changing anything at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with reason to be. Being the person who fixes the hard call does not guarantee a full paid week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you count a reopened case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count a complaint as reopened if a customer rings again after the bot says delivered. The company counts the first closure; the customer counts the parcel still missing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut if your hours fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We could stop the small Friday takeaway if my paid hours fall, but that only saves a little. I would not pretend the cut covers a missing shift.

say: I would ask our **union branch** for a written human complaints rota.
I would tell colleagues **reopened parcels** remain paid work.
think: I might retain **hard calls** while losing paid lead hours.
Our **three-week reserve** cannot absorb a missing shift for long.
do: Bring **reopened cases** to the branch meeting and request paid appeal hours with agents.
Keep **paid disputes work** when offered and get a written weekly rota; cut Friday takeaway if hours fall.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing paid hours despite my experience.
S1.quote: Being the person who fixes the hard call does not guarantee a full paid week.
fieldNote: Her **lead skill** may remain useful without protecting the whole rota.
She makes a **group request** for paid appeal hours and names a small household cut.

steps.text: Bring reopened delivery cases to union branch meeting and demand written paid appeal hours with agents
Keep paid complaints shifts when offered and request a written weekly rota
Drop Friday takeaway if her paid lead hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team that cheap thinking AI by 2028 can handle even the scan decisions we now argue over. Hands-on depot robots come later, around 2031, but my desk wages could be gone first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the company to end most of our complaint hours quickly. Sam's uneven kitchen pay and three weeks saved cannot carry the flat if my lead wage stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would ask the union branch for a group meeting on notice and final paid shifts, and put our rent, food and electricity figures on one sheet with Sam. If most of my hours end in the first year after 2028, I would ask the landlord about a payment schedule if we actually miss rent and apply for posted paid customer work only where the written weekly wage and hours cover bills after the bus fare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed; I can feel how close the rent date is. A good record on difficult calls does not put a second wage in the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask in the notice meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the last paid shift date and whether notice itself is paid. I want an answer on paper so the union can check what every worker was told.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your daughter help financially?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter could help us read an online advert, but she pays her own rent. I cannot count her wages as money we have been offered.

say: I would say **2028 thinking AI** threatens complaint decisions before 2031 depot robots.
I would ask the **union branch** for written notice and final paid-shift dates.
think: I expect **most lead hours** to end quickly.
I cannot cover the **flat's rent** from three weeks saved and Sam's uneven pay.
do: Join a **union notice meeting** to ask final paid-shift dates and whether notice is paid.
List **rent, food and electricity** with Sam; ask the landlord only if most hours end after 2028 and rent is missed.
If most 2028 hours end, apply for **posted paid work** only when written weekly wages and hours cover bills after bus fare.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by a likely large wage loss and a near rent date.
S2.quote: A good record on difficult calls does not put a second wage in the flat.
fieldNote: Her **high skill** cannot carry the household if paid lead hours end.
A **landlord schedule** is conditional on actually missing rent; adult-child wages are not assumed.

steps.text: Join union notice meeting for final paid-shift dates and whether notice is paid
If most hours end after 2028 and rent is missed, request landlord payment schedule
After most hours end, check posted paid work's written wages, hours and bus fare
Apply only if written after-fare weekly pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a few years gives the staff time to demand an honest count of paid complaint work. Thinking AI could take our desk decisions by 2031, while depot robots come around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can keep solving hard parcels for now, but I don't trust the company to keep two leads when one can supervise a screen. I might be 63 then; I do not know what income would let Sam and me stop working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask the union branch to compare monthly lead hours with the number of reopened parcels and present that request together. I would keep my paid lead shifts and build a small rent reserve when Sam has a full kitchen week; if hours fall in the first year after 2031, I would check the actual posted local wage and bus timetable before applying for another desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the extra years make a shared record possible. Our bills do not become smaller because the warning is longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put beside the rota?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring the parcel numbers as well as the rota so management cannot say fewer calls means fewer problems. It may show each complaint now needs longer to settle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop at 63?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will not call 63 a retirement date without written income figures. Sam and I can save what we can, but a thin reserve is not a promise of later pay.

say: I would ask for a **shared monthly record** of lead hours and reopened parcels.
I would say **2031 desk AI** comes before 2034 depot robots.
think: I expect my **lead hours** could shrink even while hard cases remain.
I cannot assume **retirement income** at 63 without written figures.
do: Bring **lead hours** and reopened parcels to a group union request while keeping paid shifts.
Save in **full-kitchen weeks** and check posted local wages and buses if hours fall after 2031.
feel: I feel **anxious** about wages, though time allows a shared record.
S3.quote: Our bills do not become smaller because the warning is longer.
fieldNote: She seeks **collective evidence** of paid work rather than a speculative course.
Saving depends on **Sam's shifts**, and local job enquiries follow actual hours falling.

steps.text: Join union request comparing monthly lead hours with reopened parcel counts
Keep paid parcel complaint shifts while current hours remain
Save a small rent amount only after Sam has a full kitchen week
If hours fall after 2031, check posted local wages and bus times before applying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the staff that ten years is time to organise a record of what the company actually pays, not time to be quiet. Full thinking AI reaches our desk by 2036, and depot robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I might still need a wage because our present savings would not last long. I cannot assume a pension amount or help from our daughter without seeing what is actually available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam and I would collect our real income statements and total a year of rent and bills this winter. I would keep taking paid complaints and ask the union branch to request yearly lead-hour figures; after 2036 I would keep working if verified income fails to cover the flat and the company still offers paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because rent is tight today as well as ten years from now. I can work with other leads, but I cannot talk a short wage into a long one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the annual figures show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The yearly figure should say paid hours for each lead, not just calls handled by a screen. If hours shrink, we would see it before somebody announces there are no jobs left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughter cover later bills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter is doing well enough to keep her own flat, and I want it to stay that way. We will plan with the income Sam and I can verify, not money she has never promised.

say: I would ask staff to **organise paid-hour records** across the decade.
I would tell colleagues **2036 desk AI** comes before 2039 depot robots.
think: I may still **need wages at 68** because current savings are thin.
I cannot assume a **pension amount** or my daughter's support without evidence.
do: Collect **actual income statements** with Sam and total a year of rent and bills.
Keep **paid complaints** and join union requests for annual lead hours; work after 2036 if verified income falls short.
feel: I feel **anxious** about rent now and uncertain paid work later.
S4.quote: I can work with other leads, but I cannot talk a short wage into a long one.
fieldNote: She plans around **verified income**, not an assumed pension or adult-child support.
She keeps making **shared worker demands** for paid lead-hour figures throughout the longer warning period.

steps.text: Keep taking paid parcel complaints while lead hours remain available
Join union branch request for annual paid hours for each lead
Compare Hana and Sam's income statements with annual rent and bills while keeping paid shifts

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because most of our paid desk hours could go before the next rent date. A written notice date, paid hours for human complaints and a real local opening would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what the good workers earn, not only whether they keep a title. I can lead a row and still have three weeks between our household and a late rent payment.

headlineQuote: I can lead a row and still have three weeks between our household and a late rent payment.
portrait: A **58-year-old** senior parcel complaints lead with a two-year college diploma and strong job skill.
She **never uses AI**, relying on depot scans and her ruled notebook.
Her **low lead pay** and Sam's uneven kitchen work leave only three weeks saved.
She uses **union requests** to protect paid correction hours while checking real household income.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** picture could end most desk hours before another rent date.
whatWouldHelp: A **written notice date**, paid human complaint hours and a real local opening would help.
